public_rationale: The claim has three parts: the size, the reason, and the concentration of investment. Only the reason has direct backing. Scale AI's CEO, Alexandr Wang, said on 2024-11-20 that much of the investment going into AI had been based on the belief that the scaling law would hold (The Verge, 2024-11-22). On size, a Bloomberg report published 2024-11-01 said the combined 2024 capital expenditures of Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and Alphabet were set to total well over $200 billion. The same report linked the spending to the AI boom. That figure is a projection for one year and covers all capital spending, not investment in LLM scaling specifically. So it only hints at the size the claim describes. The packet has no data on funding for non-LLM approaches. That means 'largely to the exclusion of investment in other approaches' cannot be checked. No evidence in the packet contradicts the claim.
limitations: The capex figure is a projection made in November 2024 for the full year, not a realized total.
The capex figure covers all data-center and cloud spending by four firms, not investment in LLM scaling alone, and it covers 2024 only, not 2020–2024.
The phrase 'on the assumption that I was wrong' is read as belief that scaling would keep working. Investors' views of Marcus himself cannot be observed.
Wang's statement is one industry view, and it does not quantify how much investment rested on that belief.
No measure of funding for alternative approaches was found.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Hundreds of billions of dollars went into LLM scaling on the assumption that scaling would keep working, and alternative approaches got little investment.

statement.excerpt: Hundreds of billions of dollars were invested on the assumption that I was wrong, largely to the exclusion of investment in other approaches.
statement.document_title: Satya Nadella and the three stages of scientific truth

from_speaker: Hundreds of billions of dollars were invested
on the assumption that I was wrong
largely to the exclusion of investment in other approaches
our_interpretation: Plain reading: from about 2020 to November 2024, AI investment in the hundreds of billions of dollars went mainly into scaling LLMs, on the belief that scaling would keep working. Comparatively little went to alternative approaches such as neurosymbolic AI.
'On the assumption that I was wrong' is read as 'on the assumption that scaling would keep delivering gains', since the investors' view of Marcus personally is not observable.
Three parts must hold: the size (hundreds of billions), the rationale (a belief in scaling), and the concentration (largely excluding alternatives).
criteria.support_condition: Reported totals show hundreds of billions of dollars invested in LLM/generative-AI scaling by late 2024. Industry statements tie that investment to belief in scaling laws. Funding data show alternative approaches got a small share.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Investment tied to LLM scaling was well under $100 billion by late 2024, or funding data show substantial investment in non-LLM approaches.

evidence.excerpt: The capital expenditures of the four largest internet and software companies - Amazon.com Inc., Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc. - are set to total well over $200 billion this year, a record sum for the profligate collective.
evidence.explanation: Shows spending in the hundreds of billions tied to the AI boom in 2024 alone. It is total capex, not spending on LLM scaling specifically, so it bears on the size of the claim only as context.

evidence.excerpt: Much of the investment going into AI has been based on the belief that the scaling law “would hold,” he said.
evidence.locator: paragraph beginning 'There’s a very real shift'
evidence.explanation: An industry CEO's statement that much AI investment rested on belief in scaling. This is consistent with the rationale part of the claim, but says nothing about how much went to alternatives.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A credible breakdown of realized AI investment from 2020 to November 2024 that separates LLM and generative-AI scaling from non-LLM approaches such as neurosymbolic, cognitive-architecture, or hybrid research, and shows both the dollar total for LLM scaling and the relative shares.
